ordered.title: Understanding the Premium Option
ordered.description: A rebuilt engine is the closest you can get to a new engine without paying dealer prices. It involves full disassembly, machining of the block and cylinder head, replacement of all wearing parts, and often upgraded components.

rows: ✅ Comprehensive - block decked, cylinders bored/honed, crank ground
✅ Yes - forged pistons, uprated bearings, revised oil pumps

blocks.text: In the UK engine industry, many suppliers, garages, and mechanics use "reconditioned" and "rebuilt" interchangeably. There is no legal standard that separates these terms. When we report that 70.45% of quote requests are for "reconditioned" engines [EM-VERIFIED] , a significant portion of those are actually rebuilt engines in practice - particularly for premium vehicles where upgraded components are specified. Always ask your supplier for a detailed written specification of exactly what work will be performed, regardless of what term they use.

ordered.title: The Rebuilding Process
ordered.description: Six stages from strip to test - what actually happens to your engine.

cards.title: Full Disassembly
cards.text: The engine is completely stripped down to its component parts. Every single component is removed, cleaned, and labelled.
cards.fullText: 1. Strip Full Disassembly The engine is completely stripped down to its component parts. Every single component is removed, cleaned, and labelled.

cards.title: Measure Everything
cards.text: Every component is measured against manufacturer specifications: bore wear, crank wear, cam lobes, valve guides, flatness, crack detection.
cards.fullText: 2. Inspect Measure Everything Every component is measured against manufacturer specifications: bore wear, crank wear, cam lobes, valve guides, flatness, crack detection.

cards.title: Restore to Specification
cards.text: Cylinders bored to oversize, head skimmed, crank ground, valve seats cut, block decked, oil galleries cleaned.
cards.fullText: 3. Machine Restore to Specification Cylinders bored to oversize, head skimmed, crank ground, valve seats cut, block decked, oil galleries cleaned.

cards.title: Fit Upgraded Components
cards.text: Forged pistons, uprated bearings, revised oil pumps, upgraded timing components, ARP studs/bolts (varies by builder).
cards.fullText: 4. Upgrade Fit Upgraded Components Forged pistons, uprated bearings, revised oil pumps, upgraded timing components, ARP studs/bolts (varies by builder).

cards.title: Rebuild with Precision
cards.text: New pistons, rings, bearings, timing components, oil pump, water pump, gaskets, seals. Blueprinting (if specified).
cards.fullText: 5. Assemble Rebuild with Precision New pistons, rings, bearings, timing components, oil pump, water pump, gaskets, seals. Blueprinting (if specified).

cards.title: Comprehensive Testing
cards.text: Oil pressure, compression, leak-down, engine run (cold and hot), power output, full inspection for leaks and correct operation.
cards.fullText: 6. Test Comprehensive Testing Oil pressure, compression, leak-down, engine run (cold and hot), power output, full inspection for leaks and correct operation.

ordered.title: Rebuilt vs Reconditioned - The Critical Difference
ordered.description: Understanding the difference can save you thousands and prevent disappointment.

rows: ✅ Yes - block decked, cylinders bored, crank ground

blocks.text: "The line between reconditioned and rebuilt is blurred in our industry. Some suppliers call a basic rebuild 'reconditioned.' Others call a full rebuild 'reconditioned.' The key questions are: Has the block been machined? Have the pistons been replaced? Have upgraded components been fitted? If the answer to all three is yes, it's a rebuilt engine - regardless of what the supplier calls it."

ordered.title: Core Exchange vs Send-Your-Own
ordered.description: When considering a rebuilt engine, you typically have two options. Choose the one that fits your priorities.

blocks.text: You order a rebuilt engine. The specialist sends you a rebuilt unit. You return your old engine (the "core") for a refund of the core deposit.

items: Lead time: 7-14 days
Downtime: 7-14 days (your car is waiting)
Cost: Higher upfront - includes core deposit (refundable)
Convenience: High - engine arrives ready to install
Best for: Most owners - minimises downtime

blocks.text: How it works: You pay the price plus a core deposit (£300-£1,000). The rebuilt engine is delivered. Your old engine is returned for inspection and deposit refund.
You send your existing engine to a specialist. They strip, inspect, machine, and rebuild your engine. The same engine comes back to you.

items: Lead time: 2-4 weeks (depending on workload)
Downtime: 2-4 weeks (your car is off the road)
Cost: Lower - no core deposit, often lower unit price
Convenience: Low - you need to remove and send your engine
Best for: Classic cars, enthusiasts, very rare engines, sentimental owners

blocks.text: How it works: You remove the engine (or arrange for removal). The engine is delivered to the specialist. They rebuild it and return it to you for installation.
Which option is right for you?

items: Daily driver - need the car back quickly: Core exchange - minimises downtime
Classic car - matching numbers: Send-your-own - preserves originality
Very rare engine - core units are scarce: Send-your-own - hard to find a core
Budget-conscious - saving money: Send-your-own - often cheaper (no core deposit)
Enthusiast - specific upgrades requested: Send-your-own - more control over the rebuild

ordered.title: Rebuilt Engine Risks & Caveats
ordered.description: Rebuilt engines are the premium option - but they are not without risks.

cards.text: Risk 1: Quality Varies by Builder Not all engine builders are created equal. Some cut corners - using cheap parts, skipping machining, or rushing the rebuild. Mitigation: Choose a specialist with documented experience. Ask for photos of the rebuild. Check reviews.
cards.fullText: Risk 1: Quality Varies by Builder Not all engine builders are created equal. Some cut corners - using cheap parts, skipping machining, or rushing the rebuild. Mitigation: Choose a specialist with documented experience. Ask for photos of the rebuild. Check reviews.

cards.text: Risk 2: "Rebuilt" vs "Reconditioned" Confusion Many suppliers use the terms interchangeably. You may pay for a "rebuilt" engine that is actually a "reconditioned" unit with minimal machining. Mitigation: Always ask for a detailed written specification - including machining, new pistons, and upgraded components.
cards.fullText: Risk 2: "Rebuilt" vs "Reconditioned" Confusion Many suppliers use the terms interchangeably. You may pay for a "rebuilt" engine that is actually a "reconditioned" unit with minimal machining. Mitigation: Always ask for a detailed written specification - including machining, new pistons, and upgraded components.

cards.text: Risk 3: Core Deposit Disputes If the specialist deems your old engine "unrebuildable," they may withhold part or all of the deposit. Mitigation: Clarify core return conditions before ordering. What constitutes a "rebuildable" core? What are the conditions for a full refund?
cards.fullText: Risk 3: Core Deposit Disputes If the specialist deems your old engine "unrebuildable," they may withhold part or all of the deposit. Mitigation: Clarify core return conditions before ordering. What constitutes a "rebuildable" core? What are the conditions for a full refund?

cards.text: Risk 4: Fitment Quality A rebuilt engine is only as good as the installation. Poor fitting can cause oil leaks, coolant leaks, premature wear, or immediate failure. Mitigation: Use a reputable garage with experience in your engine type. Ask the supplier for fitting recommendations.
cards.fullText: Risk 4: Fitment Quality A rebuilt engine is only as good as the installation. Poor fitting can cause oil leaks, coolant leaks, premature wear, or immediate failure. Mitigation: Use a reputable garage with experience in your engine type. Ask the supplier for fitting recommendations.

cards.text: Risk 5: Break-In Period Rebuilt engines require a break-in period. If you fail to follow procedures, you may void the warranty and cause premature wear. Mitigation: Follow the break-in instructions provided by the builder. Use the recommended oil. Don't drive hard until the engine is fully run in.
cards.fullText: Risk 5: Break-In Period Rebuilt engines require a break-in period. If you fail to follow procedures, you may void the warranty and cause premature wear. Mitigation: Follow the break-in instructions provided by the builder. Use the recommended oil. Don't drive hard until the engine is fully run in.

ordered.title: How Engines Market Works
ordered.description: Four simple steps to get your rebuilt engine.

blocks.text: Enter your vehicle registration. We identify your exact make, model, year, and engine code. You can also describe the failure.
Your enquiry is shared with 100+ vetted UK specialists. Within 30-60 minutes, you'll receive 3-5 quotes from suppliers who have your engine in stock - including rebuilt options.
Review quotes side-by-side. Compare price, warranty, what's included, lead time, and supplier reviews. No obligation to accept any quote.
Select the option that fits your budget and timeline. Payment is made directly to the supplier. Engines Market never handles money. Your engine is delivered or fitted.

Data sharing: Your contact details are shared with a maximum of 10 suppliers (GDPR compliance). Suppliers see your vehicle, postcode region, and failure description. They cannot see your contact details until they choose to "unlock" the lead.

blocks.question: How much does a rebuilt engine cost in the UK? −
blocks.answer: Rebuilt engines cost £3,000-£5,000 supply only or £4,500-£7,500 fitted . Prices vary by engine type, vehicle segment, and regional labour rates. Premium and performance engines cost significantly more.

blocks.question: What's the difference between rebuilt and reconditioned? +
blocks.answer: In the UK engine industry, many suppliers use "reconditioned" and "rebuilt" interchangeably. There is no legal standard that separates these terms. A true rebuilt engine typically includes comprehensive machining, new pistons, and upgraded components. Always ask for a detailed written specification.

blocks.question: Is a rebuilt engine worth the extra cost over a reconditioned one? +
blocks.answer: For vehicles worth over £15,000 that you plan to keep 3+ years - yes. The upgraded components and longer warranty justify the extra cost. For most vehicles worth under £15,000, a reconditioned engine is better value.

blocks.question: What warranty comes with a rebuilt engine? +
blocks.answer: Rebuilt engines typically carry a 12-24 month warranty covering parts and labour on internal mechanical failure. Some specialists offer longer warranties for premium rebuilds.

blocks.question: How long does a rebuilt engine take? +
blocks.answer: Lead time is typically 7-14 days for a core exchange, or 2-4 weeks if you send your own engine. This includes stripping, inspecting, machining, rebuilding, and testing.

blocks.question: What's the difference between core exchange and send-your-own? +
blocks.answer: Core exchange: You order a rebuilt engine and return your old engine for a deposit refund. Quicker. Send-your-own: You send your engine to the specialist. Slower but preserves matching numbers. Choose based on your priorities.

blocks.question: Can I fit a rebuilt engine myself? +
blocks.answer: We strongly recommend professional fitting. Rebuilt engines are precision units that require correct installation - incorrect fitting can void the warranty and cause premature failure.

blocks.question: What should I ask a rebuilt engine supplier before buying? +
blocks.answer: Detailed written specification of work performed. Photos of the rebuild. Warranty terms (length, parts & labour, exclusions). What upgraded components are fitted. Core deposit terms. Break-in procedures. Fitting recommendations.

blocks.question: Do I need to tell the DVLA and my insurer? +
blocks.answer: DVLA - update the engine number on your V5C. Insurer - you should check with your insurer. Some policies require notification of major mechanical changes, while others may not.
